title: Private VPC Networking Deep Dive - Runtime & Networking
summary: Deep dive focused on networking design for Redwood Private VPC deployments and runtime performance tradeoffs. Covered PrivateLink architecture, egress/NAT options, subnet placement for dedicated inference hosts, DNS resolution considerations, and how KV cache/batching/quantization affect tail latency and throughput. Action items and benchmark plan agreed.

transcript:
Meeting: Private VPC Networking Deep Dive - Runtime & Networking
Date: 2026-06-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 60m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Acme Platform), Maya (Acme Security), Ethan (Acme ML Infra)

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, I think we've got an hour. quick goal for today — pair on network topology for Private VPC, and then dig into runtime perf implications (kv cache locality, batching, quant). sorry if i talk fast, been a long week.

[00:18] Jordan: no worries, thanks Alex. we're most interested in how you'll integrate w/ our VPC, egress constraints, and also what the latency profile would look like if we colocate dedicated hosts in our private subnets.

[00:30] Priya: yep and I'll try to map the runtime pieces to the network: where the KV cache lives, how we do prefix cache hits, and where batching boundaries are. quick question for the team — are you planning to use PrivateLink or a Transit GW for connectivity?

[00:45] Maya: our security policy prefers PrivateLink where possible — it minimizes exposure. Transit GW is allowed but needs extra review. also we have strict egress control and no direct internet egress from our model subnets unless it's via approved NAT/proxy.

[01:05] Alex: understood. PrivateLink is supported by Redwood Private: we expose an interface endpoint (AWS ENI) in the customer's VPC and run the control plane over that PrivateLink. data plane options: for dedicated pools we can either place inference nodes inside the customer's private subnets (we call that customer-hosted Dedicated) or run them in Redwood-managed subnet with PrivateLink to the customer — tradeoffs there.

[01:28] Ethan: can you unpack the tradeoffs? especially for KV cache locality — does having hosts in your network vs ours change cache hit latency significantly?

[01:40] Priya: good question. short answer: yes. If inference workers and the KV cache (prefix and attention cache) are in the same subnet/az, you get single-digit ms local latency. If the KV cache is across PrivateLink, you add extra hops + ENI costs and typically see additional 3–8 ms depending on routing and security groups. for large context workloads the extra ms per token can add up.

[02:05] Jordan: hmm that latency adds up for streaming chat. our SLOs are 150 ms tail for 2k tokens — is that realistic with PrivateLink?

[02:15] Priya: it's doable with careful batching and ensuring KV cache locality. A pattern we recommend: run inference workers in customer-controlled subnets (we deploy as a private agent inside your VPC) so the KV cache and runtime are local; control plane still uses PrivateLink for orchestration. That eliminates the cross-vpc data hops. If that's not possible, we optimize by pinning model shards to the same AZ as the interface endpoint and use local NLBs to reduce path length.

[02:42] Maya: that private agent approach — does it require inbound ports open? we're strict about inbound.

[02:50] Alex: no inbound from internet. The agent initiates outbound connections to Redwood control plane over the PrivateLink. For management we propose a management ENI that sits in a management subnet. Runtime traffic between Redwood components and your inference workers stays inside your VPC. We can provide Terraform snippets for security group rules — typically only allow Encrypted TLS outbound to specific Redwood endpoints.

[03:18] Ethan: ok what about NAT/egress? we force all model subnets to egress through our egress proxies for audit. Does Redwood need any outbound internet access from the model hosts?

[03:28] Priya: for typical inference upates and telemetry, no public internet is required if PrivateLink is used for control plane and we push images via a customer-managed registry. If image pulling from our registry is required, we can mirror images into ECR in your account or provide a signed image bundle via your artifact repo. For telemetry, we can optionally send logs to your SIEM via syslog/forwarder in your VPC.

[03:58] Jordan: good. can you explain DNS concerns — split horizon and internal name resolution, because we run an internal DNS that blocks external hostnames by default.

[04:08] Priya: yeah DNS is a common gotcha. For PrivateLink we recommend creating VPC interface endpoints which resolve to private DNS names. You may need to enable "enablePrivateDnsName" so that the standard service FQNs resolve to the private IPs. If you have split-horizon DNS, you need to add conditional forwarders or private hosted zones so that internal services (e.g., model store) resolve correctly. We'll share a short checklist.

[04:36] Maya: will the REDWOOD product call external model downloading endpoints? we can't allow that without review.

[04:44] Alex: no — model artifacts are either hosted in your registry or in Redwood artifacts in a private S3 with a VPC gateway endpoint. We can do cross-account roles and presigned URLs limited to your VPC.

[04:58] Ethan: let's talk runtime perf tradeoffs: batching and tail latency. if we enable larger batches to improve throughput, what happens to our 95/99 latency?

[05:08] Priya: batching increases throughput but can increase *head* latency for the first token in a request if we wait for the batch window. We do continuous batching — low-latency mode uses small batch sizes and strict batching windows to keep p99 tight, but it reduces overall throughput. We recommend adaptive batching: start in low-latency, then auto-scale to moderate batch sizes when QPS increases. Also, prefix caching reduces per-token compute for repeated prefixes and can significantly reduce median latency for chatty sessions.

[05:40] Jordan: quantify please — e.g., under medium load, what's the p50/p95 for a 2k prompt using a 13B model with int8 quant?

[05:48] Priya: approximate numbers: with local inference hosts and KV cache warmed, median token latency ~8–12 ms; p95 ~40–80 ms depending on sequence length and attention recompute; p99 can hit 150–300 ms if KV cache cold or if we have tail QPS spikes. With cross-vpc PrivateLink added hop, add ~3–8 ms to median and the p95/p99 bands widen a bit. Quantization (int8) reduces compute time by ~20–35% but can slightly increase CPU overhead for dequant/decode depending on kernel. We'll include benchmark artifacts.

[06:28] Maya: that p99 sounds high for us — we need to keep 99 under 200ms for interactive flows. can dedicated reserved capacity help?

[06:36] Priya: yes reserved dedicated capacity ensures worker pool saturation is controlled, reduces cold-starts, and keeps KV cache resident. Also pinning shards to GPUs and prewarming KV cache for expected prompts helps. If you expect adversarial bursts, we recommend a small overprovision buffer and an autoscale policy with burst capacity.

[06:58] Ethan: about quantization — are you doing per-channel quant or dynamic? how much quality delta should we expect on our evals?

[07:06] Priya: we use quant profiles per model: symmetric per-channel for weights and dynamic per-tensor activations (int8). For many open LLMs quality is preserved within a small delta; for some safety-critical prompts you might see a regression. Redwood Optimize will run evals on your prompt sets and produce quality-vs-cost tradeoff recommendations. We can run a QC pass with your evals as part of the pilot.

[07:36] Jordan: back to networking — what about cross-account IAM roles and flow logs? we need full auditability.

[07:44] Alex: flow logs and VPC logs are fully supported. We can integrate with your CloudTrail and Flow Logs; we ask for a read-only role to pull audit records, or we can accept pushed logs to an S3 we control but in your account. We also support KMS/HSM integration for model keys and customer secrets — we can wrap keys in either your KMS or a dedicated HSM in Redwood-managed flow if required.

[08:12] Maya: ok strengths. one more on PrivateLink: do you require endpoint service acceptance, or can we create our own interface endpoints to your service?

[08:22] Alex: we publish an endpoint-service in our AWS account; you create an interface endpoint and accept the connection. For cross-region, we support regional endpoints; if you prefer a partner-managed approach we can do that too. We'll share the exact ARN and the required service name.

[08:38] Ethan: curious about NIC throughput — if we put inference in our subnet, do you deploy GPU instances as ENIs attached to our subnets? what's the network footprint per model?

[08:48] Priya: we deploy inference workers as EC2/GKE nodes in your VPC (or their analog on Azure/GCP). Network footprint is modest per request — the heavy work is local on the GPU memory. For KV cache access and parameter server sharding across machines, you get cross-node traffic; we recommend keeping shards within AZ and using enhanced networking. For sharded models, prefer instance types with GPU-attached NVLink to reduce cross-host traffic. We'll provide a recommended instance sizing guide per model family.

[09:18] Jordan: great. can you outline a pilot (what we'll measure)?

[09:24] Priya: pilot outline: 1) deploy a small dedicated pool in your dev account (one AZ, 2–4 GPU nodes), 2) run two benchmark workloads — long-context streaming chat and short-shot batch inference, 3) measure p50/p95/p99 token latencies, throughput (tokens/s), KV cache hit rates, and network-level RTTs, 4) run quantized vs non-quantized profiles and compare quality metrics on your evals. We'll collect logs and produce a perf report.

[09:56] Maya: sounds good. who owns the infra changes? we want minimal changes to our infra team.

[10:02] Alex: Redwood SE will provide IaC and a step-by-step runbook. We'll do the deployment together with Ethan and Jordan, and Priya will run the perf harness. We aim for a 1-week pilot once infra exceptions and approvals are in place.

[10:18] Jordan: any docs re: security hardening for the agent?

[10:22] Priya: yes we'll send our security hardening checklist: least privilege IAM, sg rules, no public inbound, ECR image scanning, optional FIPS/TLS profiles, and KMS integration steps.

[10:34] Maya: ok last question — DNS TTL and cache invalidation during model rollouts? we prefer low TTLs for quick rollback capability.

[10:42] Alex: we recommend using stable model IDs and control-plane-driven rollouts rather than DNS changes. That's more deterministic. If you must use DNS, set low TTLs and ensure your internal resolver honors them; otherwise, use proxy-based routing inside the VPC.

[10:58] Alex: all right let's recap real quick — action items: Redwood share network diagrams, Terraform snippets, and pilot plan; Redwood runs perf benchmarks; Acme sends egress/dns/compliance constraints. we'll schedule the pilot kickoff next wednesday 10am your time. any objections?

[11:18] Maya: no objections. thanks everyone.

[11:22] Jordan: thanks, appreciate the level of detail.

[11:25] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and calendar invite. bye.

[11:30] — end of recording —
